The Rufous-capped thornbill (Chalcostigma ruficeps) is a diminutive high-altitude hummingbird whose life history is characterized by several precise developmental milestones. Laboratory measurements on captive individuals indicate that incubation at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] yields an incubation period lasting exactly 15 days [ab = 15 days]. This relatively short embryonic phase, typical of small trochilids, gives rise to a hatchling with an initial body mass of only 0.43 grams [Ww0 = 0.43 grams]. This neonatal weight, derived from comparative data on the speckled hummingbird Adelomyia melanogenys, reflects the extreme miniaturization required for adult females to sustain flight while carrying developing eggs, and it establishes a baseline from which the nestling’s rapid growth trajectory can be assessed over the subsequent weeks of parental care.

Under the physiological thermal regime characteristic of active hummingbirds, approximately 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the developmental schedule unfolds in a predictable sequence. The altricial nestling begins its first exogenous feeding shortly after hatching and experiences a period of rapid feather growth and mass gain, culminating in the ability to fly at 17 days after hatching [tx = 17 days after hatching] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Fledging at this age marks a critical transition from complete dependency on the provisioning adult to a phase of gradually increasing locomotor independence. This relatively brief nestling period—among the shortest recorded for Andean hummingbirds of comparable body size—is likely an adaptation that minimizes predation risk in the exposed montane environment where the species breeds.

Under the same thermal conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the onset of sexual maturation occurs at 51 days after hatching [tp = 51 days after hatching]. This rapid attainment of gonadal activity allows individuals to become potential breeders within their first season, a life-history strategy that capitalizes on short windows of resource abundance in the high Andes. The species exhibits a clear sexual size dimorphism in terms of ultimate body mass: adult females reach a stable wet weight of 3 grams [Wwi = 3 grams], whereas adult males achieve a larger ultimate wet weight of 3.8 grams [Wwi = 3.8 grams]. This difference likely reflects sexual selection pressures on male body size for territorial defense of flowering patches.

Despite reaching puberty early, the species does not immediately engage in reproduction; instead, first breeding is deferred. The first brood or nesting event does not occur until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a full year post-hatching, when the individual has had time to consolidate its territory and accumulate sufficient energy reserves for the demanding process of egg production and incubation at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. The reproductive output is modest and finely tuned to the unpredictable nectar availability at elevation. Each breeding event consists of a single clutch containing exactly two eggs [N_R_i = Each breeding event consists of a single clutch containing exactly two eggs]. Furthermore, females typically produce just one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a conservative reproductive rate that prioritizes offspring quality and parental survival over high fecundity.

The species’ maximum recorded longevity under field conditions, measured at the characteristic active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years]. This lifespan is relatively extended for a hummingbird of such diminutive size and is consistent with a slow-paced life history that includes deferred reproduction and a low annual reproductive output. In terms of metabolic investment, respirometry studies conducted at the same regulated body temperature of 38.1 °C have recorded a peak resting metabolic rate of 27.27 milliliters per hour [JOi = 27.27 milliliters per hour] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This basal oxygen consumption reflects the elevated energetic demands of maintaining endothermy in a small body, and it underscores the necessity of frequent nectar feeding to sustain the high metabolic machinery that supports this bird’s rapid development, flight, and extended lifespan.
